implementation_notes: On the JVM, Kotlin compiles to the same intrinsic monitors as Java: the synchronized function and the @Synchronized annotation are the monitor lock and wait/notify/notifyAll on java.lang.Object are the monitor condition, so a class with @Synchronized methods is a monitor object with no extra machinery, and a withLock helper keeps the critical section scoped. The catch is portability: these APIs exist only on the JVM target, so a shared-state class written this way is not multiplatform Kotlin. For code that must not block a thread, kotlinx.coroutines.Mutex - a suspending lock - is the documented alternative, and confinement to a single-threaded dispatcher is the cheapest option of all and is what UI code uses.
pitfalls: wait/notify are reachable only through a java.lang.Object cast and exist only on the JVM; common, JS and native targets have no intrinsic monitors, so this realisation cannot be shared in multiplatform code.

@Synchronized locks the instance (or the Class object for @JvmStatic methods): external code locking the same instance reintroduces the coupling, and blocking inside the monitor on a single-threaded dispatcher deadlocks outright.
Coroutine code must not call blocking monitor methods: mixing a blocking monitor with suspending callers can pin a dispatcher thread and deadlock, which is why Mutex exists.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex and confinement
variants.implementation_notes: The coroutine documentation contrasts the blocking world (synchronized, ReentrantLock) with Mutex, whose lock() is a suspending function and therefore does not block a thread; withLock { } wraps the critical section and the state is protected across suspensions. Because Mutex has no condition variables, a method that must wait for a predicate either re-checks after awaiting a channel/flow, or the state is confined to a single-threaded context (or an actor-style channel loop) and every method becomes a suspending message - the confinement route serialises without any lock at all and is what the docs recommend for coarse-grained state.
pitfalls: Mutex is not reentrant: a nested withLock on the same Mutex suspends forever, so interface and implementation methods must be split as with any monitor.

Only cooperating code is protected: a path that touches the shared state without the mutex (or from another dispatcher without confinement) breaks the guarantee silently, with no memory barrier and no compiler help.
Never block inside a coroutine-held mutex (Thread.sleep, blocking I/O): it pins the dispatcher thread the mutex is protecting and can deadlock every coroutine on that dispatcher.
